summary: Emil Kowalski argues that good animation is not an innate art but a set of learnable tricks, and gives seven concrete ones. Buttons should scale down slightly when pressed, enter animations should not start from scale(0), and once one tooltip is open the next ones should open with no delay and no animation. Easing is the most important part of an animation: anything entering or exiting the screen should use ease-out, ideally a custom curve stronger than CSS's built-ins, and never ease-in. Popovers should scale in from their trigger, UI animations should stay fast (generally under 300ms) or be removed when seen tens or hundreds of times a day, and a little blur can hide a transition that still feels off. For a design system, these translate into motion tokens (durations, easing curves, starting scale), component behaviour (tooltip delay, origin-aware popovers, press feedback) and a polish checklist [inferred].
key_ideas: The interface should feel like it is listening: every user action gets feedback as soon as possible.
A subtle press scale (0.97) makes buttons feel instantly more responsive.
Starting an animation from scale(0) looks like the element comes from nowhere; start at 0.9 or higher.
Tooltips need an initial delay, but once one is open, neighbouring tooltips should open with no delay and no animation.
Easing is the most important part of any animation; it can make a bad animation look great and a great one look bad.
Use ease-out for anything entering or exiting the screen; ease-in starts slow and feels slower at the same duration.
Built-in CSS easing curves are usually too weak; custom curves feel more energetic.
Popovers should scale in from their trigger, so transform-origin must not be left at its default center.
Unseen details compound: users may not consciously notice them, but in aggregate they make the product feel better.
Fast animations improve perceived performance; keep UI animations under 300ms as a rule of thumb.
Animations and hover effects seen tens or hundreds of times a day should be removed because they become annoying.
When easing and duration tweaks still leave a transition feeling off, a small blur can bridge the old and new states.

topics.name: Motion principles
topics.summary: Seven practical tips: press feedback, no scale(0), instant subsequent tooltips, ease-out, origin-aware popovers, fast or no animation, and blur as a last resort.

topics.name: Easing and timing
topics.summary: Easing is the most important part of an animation; use ease-out (preferably custom) for enter and exit, avoid ease-in, keep UI animations under 300ms, and 180ms feels more responsive than 400ms.

topics.name: Micro-interactions

topics.name: Buttons and actions

rules.rule: Give the user feedback on every action as soon as possible, so the interface feels like it is listening.
rules.why: The interface should feel as if it's listening to the user.
rules.evidence: You should aim to give the user feedback on all of their actions as soon as possible

rules.rule: Show a loading state when a form is submitted.
rules.why: Every action should get feedback as soon as possible.
rules.evidence: Submitting a form should show a loading state

rules.rule: Show a success state after a copy-to-clipboard action.
rules.why: Every action should get feedback as soon as possible.
rules.evidence: copy to clipboard action should show a success state

rules.rule: Scale buttons down subtly while pressed: scale 0.97 on the :active pseudo-class.
rules.why: It is an easy way to make the interface feel instantly more responsive.
rules.evidence: A scale of 0.97 on the :active pseudo-class should do the job

rules.rule: Do not animate an element in from scale(0).
rules.why: Elements that animate from scale(0) can make an animation feel off; it looks like the element comes out of nowhere.
rules.evidence: Elements that animate from scale(0) can make an animation feel off

rules.rule: Start scale-in animations from an initial scale of 0.9 or higher (the article's example uses 0.93).
rules.why: A higher initial scale feels more gentle, natural and elegant and resembles the real world, like a deflated balloon that still has a shape.
rules.evidence: Try animating from a higher initial scale instead (0.9+)

rules.rule: Give tooltips a delay before they first appear.
rules.why: The delay prevents accidental activation.
rules.evidence: Tooltips should have a delay before appearing to prevent accidental activation

rules.rule: Once a tooltip is open, open other tooltips in the same group immediately, with no delay and no animation.
rules.why: It feels faster without defeating the purpose of the initial delay.
rules.evidence: Once a tooltip is open, hovering over other tooltips should open them with no delay and no animation

rules.rule: In Base UI, disable the animation on subsequent tooltips by targeting the data-instant attribute and setting transition-duration to 0ms.
rules.why: Base UI skips the delay itself; this also skips the animation for subsequent tooltips.
rules.evidence: target the data-instant attribute and set the transition duration to 0ms

rules.rule: Animate tooltips in and out with transform and opacity at 0.125s ease-out, starting and ending at opacity 0 and scale(0.97), with transform-origin set from the library variable.

rules.evidence: Here’s how the styles would look like to achieve this

rules.rule: Treat easing as the most important part of any animation when building or reviewing motion.
rules.why: Easing can make a bad animation look great and a great animation look bad.
rules.evidence: Easing ... is the most important part of any animation

rules.rule: Use ease-out for anything entering or exiting the screen.
rules.why: It accelerates at the beginning, which gives the user a feeling of responsiveness.
rules.evidence: If you are animating something that is entering or exiting the screen, use ease-out

rules.rule: Pick easing that moves fast at the beginning of the motion and does not speed up at the end.
rules.why: Ease-out moves much faster at the beginning, which is what UI animations want; ease-in speeds up at the end, which is the opposite of what we want.
rules.evidence: Notice how much faster it moves at the beginning, that’s what we want for our animations

rules.rule: Do not use ease-in for UI animations such as dropdowns.
rules.why: It starts slow and speeds up at the end, the opposite of what UI needs; at the same 300ms it feels slower than ease-out.
rules.evidence: this easing is just not made for UI animations. It speeds up at the end

rules.rule: Do not try to rescue ease-in by shortening the duration; switch the curve instead.
rules.why: Decreasing the duration could make ease-in work, but the curve itself is not made for UI animations.
rules.evidence: You could decrease the duration to make ease-in work

rules.rule: Avoid the built-in CSS easing curves; use custom easing curves instead.
rules.why: The built-in curves are usually not strong enough; a custom curve feels more energetic.
rules.evidence: The built-in easing curves in CSS are usually not strong enough, which is why I almost never use them

rules.rule: Apply the easing principles with a custom, stronger ease-out curve for more impact.
rules.why: Custom easing feels more energetic than the built-in version of the same curve.

rules.evidence: here’s one I recommend: easings.co

rules.rule: Make popovers origin-aware: scale them in from their trigger by setting transform-origin to the trigger side.
rules.why: It makes popovers feel better; the difference is most noticeable when both horizontal and vertical origins differ, like top right.
rules.evidence: 5. Make your animations origin-aware

rules.rule: Check origin-aware popovers at a position where both the horizontal and vertical origins differ from center, such as top right.

rules.why: The default value center is wrong in most cases.

rules.evidence: A 180ms select animation feels more responsive than a 400ms one

decisions.question: Which easing curve should elements entering or leaving the screen use?

options.name: ease-in
options.effect: Starts slow and speeds up at the end; a 300ms dropdown feels slower than the same one with ease-out.
options.when: Not for UI enter or exit animations, per the source.

options.name: Built-in ease-out
options.effect: Starts fast, so the UI feels responsive, but the built-in curve is usually not strong enough.
options.when: Follows the ease-out principle, but the source prefers a custom curve for more impact.

options.name: Custom ease-out
options.effect: Starts fast with more energy and impact than the built-in keyword.
options.when: Default for enter and exit animations.

decisions.recommendation: Custom ease-out: ease-out accelerates at the start, which feels responsive, and custom curves are stronger than CSS's built-ins.

decisions.question: What scale should a popover, menu or other element start from when it animates in?

options.name: scale(0)
options.effect: The element appears to come out of nowhere and the animation feels off.

options.name: 0.9 or higher (e.g. 0.93)

decisions.question: Where should popovers and dropdowns scale from?

options.name: Center (CSS default)

options.name: Origin-aware (from the trigger)

process.detail: Scale buttons to 0.97 on :active; show a loading state on form submit and a success state on copy to clipboard.
Replace any scale(0) entrance with an initial scale of 0.9 or higher (e.g. 0.93).
Keep an initial delay on the first tooltip; open subsequent tooltips with no delay and no animation (Base UI: [data-instant] transition-duration 0ms).
Use ease-out for anything entering or exiting; replace ease-in and built-in keywords with a custom ease-out curve (e.g. from easings.co).
Make popovers scale from their trigger by setting transform-origin from the library variable instead of the default center; the difference shows most at a top-right position.
Keep UI animations under 300ms; remove animations and hover effects on elements seen tens or hundreds of times a day.

process.step: Use blur as the last resort
process.detail: Only after trying a few easings and durations, add a small filter: blur() (e.g. 2px) to crossfades that still feel off.

caveats: Self-promotion: the page opens with a plug for the aiforui.dev course (early access closed) and ends with a waitlist plug for animations.dev.
Publication date is unknown, so library behaviour (Radix and Base UI tooltip delay skipping, data-instant, CSS variable names) may have changed since.
The Radix variable shown is the dropdown-menu one (--radix-dropdown-menu-content-transform-origin); the article does not list the variable names for other Radix components.

The article relies on interactive demos (labelled Paste, Options, Feedback, Ethereum); the scraped text only has their labels and captions, so visual comparisons are described from the surrounding prose.
The code snippets were scraped with extra spaces (e.g. '0.125 s', 'var ( --transform-origin )'); values are normalised here without changing any numbers.
The 300ms ceiling is stated as a rule of thumb ('generally'), not a hard limit; 180ms vs 400ms is a single demo comparison.
No specific custom cubic-bezier values are given; the article defers to easings.co for custom curves.

maps_to is null for every decision: the questionnaire's motion questions ask about duration steps (Q-motion-02) and curve grouping (Q-motion-03), not the specific choices this article makes, so none clearly matches.
